claim: A third (33%, 3379/10263) of hippocampal neurons (dentate gyrus, CA3, CA1 and subiculum) showed movie-selectivity.
source: Surprisingly, a third (33%, 3379/10263) of hippocampal –dentate gyrus, CA3, CA1 and subiculum– neurons showed movie-selectivity, with elevated firing in specific movie sub-segments, termed movie-fields, similar to the vast majority of thalamo-cortical (LGN, V1, AM-PM) neurons (97%, 6554/6785).
evidence: The abstract provides specific quantitative data (33%, 3379/10263) from the experimental results.

claim: The vast majority (97%, 6554/6785) of thalamo-cortical (LGN, V1, AM-PM) neurons showed movie-selectivity.
source: Surprisingly, a third (33%, 3379/10263) of hippocampal –dentate gyrus, CA3, CA1 and subiculum– neurons showed movie-selectivity, with elevated firing in specific movie sub-segments, termed movie-fields, similar to the vast majority of thalamo-cortical (LGN, V1, AM-PM) neurons (97%, 6554/6785).
evidence: The abstract provides specific quantitative data (97%, 6554/6785) from the experimental results.

claim: Movie-tuning remained intact in immobile or spontaneously running mice.
source: Movie-tuning remained intact in immobile or spontaneously running mice.
evidence: The abstract states this finding directly from the experimental observations.

claim: Visual neurons had >5 movie-fields per cell.
source: Visual neurons had >5 movie-fields per cell, but only ~2 in hippocampus.
evidence: The abstract provides quantitative comparison of movie-fields between visual and hippocampal neurons.

claim: Hippocampal neurons had only ~2 movie-fields per cell.
source: Visual neurons had >5 movie-fields per cell, but only ~2 in hippocampus.
evidence: The abstract provides quantitative comparison of movie-fields between visual and hippocampal neurons.

claim: Movie-field durations in all brain regions spanned an unprecedented 1000-fold range: from 0.02s to 20s.
source: The movie-field durations in all brain regions spanned an unprecedented 1000-fold range: from 0.02s to 20s, termed mega-scale coding.
evidence: The abstract provides specific quantitative measurements of movie-field duration ranges.

claim: The total duration of all the movie-fields of a cell was comparable across neurons and brain regions.
source: Yet, the total duration of all the movie-fields of a cell was comparable across neurons and brain regions.
evidence: The abstract states this finding from comparative analysis across brain regions.

claim: Hippocampal responses showed greater continuous-sequence encoding than visual areas, as evidenced by fewer and broader movie-fields than in visual areas.
source: The hippocampal responses thus showed greater continuous-sequence encoding than visual areas, as evidenced by fewer and broader movie-fields than in visual areas.
evidence: The abstract provides an interpretation based on comparative data between hippocampal and visual areas.

claim: Repeated presentation of the movie images in a fixed, but scrambled sequence virtually abolished hippocampal but not visual-cortical selectivity.
source: Consistently, repeated presentation of the movie images in a fixed, but scrambled sequence virtually abolished hippocampal but not visual-cortical selectivity.
evidence: The abstract describes experimental results from the scrambled sequence condition.

claim: The preference for continuous, compared to scrambled sequence was eight-fold greater in hippocampal than visual areas.
source: The preference for continuous, compared to scrambled sequence was eight-fold greater in hippocampal than visual areas, further supporting episodic-sequence encoding.
evidence: The abstract provides quantitative comparison (eight-fold) from experimental data.

claim: Primary visual cortical responses are direction selective.
source: In addition to the position and orientation of simple visual cues, like Gabor patches and drifting gratings (Hubel and Wiesel, 1959), primary visual cortical responses are also direction selective (De Valois et al., 1982), and show predictive coding (Xu et al., 2012), suggesting that the temporal sequence of visual cues influences neural firing.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to De Valois et al., 1982.

claim: Primary visual cortical responses show predictive coding.
source: In addition to the position and orientation of simple visual cues, like Gabor patches and drifting gratings (Hubel and Wiesel, 1959), primary visual cortical responses are also direction selective (De Valois et al., 1982), and show predictive coding (Xu et al., 2012), suggesting that the temporal sequence of visual cues influences neural firing.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Xu et al., 2012.

claim: Visual cortical neurons encode a sequence of visual images (a movie).
source: Accordingly, these as well as higher visual cortical neurons encode a sequence of visual images, i.e., a movie (de Vries et al., 2020; Yen et al., 2007; Herikstad et al., 2011; Vinje and Gallant, 2000; Froudarakis et al., 2014; Hoseini et al., 2019; Herikstad et al., 2011; Kampa et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior studies.

claim: The hippocampus is farthest downstream from the retina in the visual circuit.
source: The hippocampus is farthest downstream from the retina in the visual circuit.
evidence: This is a statement based on established neuroanatomical knowledge.

claim: Rodent hippocampal place cells encode spatial or temporal sequences.
source: The rodent hippocampal place cells encode spatial or temporal sequences (MacDonald et al., 2011; Mehta et al., 2000; Mehta and Wilson, 2000; Mehta, 2015; Mehta et al., 1997; Buzsáki and Moser, 2013; Mau et al., 2018; Kraus et al., 2015; Kraus et al., 2013; O'Keefe and Nadel, 1978) and episode-like responses (Pastalkova et al., 2008; Moore et al., 2021; Buzsáki and Tingley, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior studies.

claim: Hippocampal responses typically require active locomotion.
source: However, these responses typically require active locomotion (McNaughton et al., 1996), and they are thought to be non-sensory responses (O'Keefe and Dostrovsky, 1971).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to McNaughton et al., 1996.

claim: Hippocampal responses are thought to be non-sensory responses.
source: However, these responses typically require active locomotion (McNaughton et al., 1996), and they are thought to be non-sensory responses (O'Keefe and Dostrovsky, 1971).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to O'Keefe and Dostrovsky, 1971.

claim: Primate and human hippocampal responses are selective to specific sets of visual cues.
source: Primate and human hippocampal responses are selective to specific sets of visual cues, e.g., the objectplace association (Parkinson et al., 1988), their short-term (Scoville and Milber, 1957) and long-term (Quiroga et al., 2005) memories, cognitive boundaries between episodic movies (Zheng et al., 2022), and event integration for narrative association (Cohn-Sheehy et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior studies.

claim: The hippocampal encoding of a continuous sequence of images (a visual episode) is unknown.
source: However, despite strong evidence for the role of hippocampus in episodic memory, the hippocampal encoding of a continuous sequence of images, i.e., a visual episode, is unknown.
evidence: This statement identifies a gap in current knowledge based on the literature review.

claim: Mice were monocularly shown a 30-s clip of a continuous segment from the movie Touch of Evil.
source: Mice were monocularly shown a 30-s clip of a continuous segment from the movie Touch of Evil (Welles, 1958) (Siegle et al., 2021; Figure 1—figure supplement 1 and Figure 1—video 1).
evidence: This describes the experimental protocol used in the study.

claim: Mice were head-fixed but were free to run on a circular disk.
source: Mice were head-fixed but were free to run on a circular disk.
evidence: This describes the experimental setup.

claim: A total of 17,048 broad spiking, active, putatively excitatory neurons were analyzed, recorded using 4–6 Neuropixel probes in 24 sessions from 24 mice.
source: A total of 17,048 broad spiking, active, putatively excitatory neurons were analyzed, recorded using 4–6 Neuropixel probes in 24 sessions from 24 mice (see Methods).
evidence: This provides specific quantitative details about the dataset analyzed.

claim: The majority of neurons in the visual areas (LGN, V1, AM–PM) were modulated by the movie.
source: The majority of neurons in the visual areas (lateral geniculate nucleus [LGN], primary visual cortex [V1], higher visual areas: antero-medial and posterior-medial [AM–PM]) were modulated by the movie, consistent with previous reports (Figure 1—figure supplement 2; de Vries et al., 2020; Yen et al., 2007; Herikstad et al., 2011; Vinje and Gallant, 2000; Froudarakis et al., 2014; Hoseini et al., 2019; Kampa et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2 and citations to prior studies.

claim: V1 (97.3%) and AM–PM (97.1%) had the largest percentage of movie-tuned cells.
source: The areas V1 (97.3%) and AM–PM (97.1%) had the largest percentage of movie-tuned cells.
evidence: This provides specific quantitative results from the analysis.

claim: The majority of neurons in LGN (89.2%) showed significant modulation by the movie.
source: Similarly, the majority of neurons in LGN (89.2%) too showed significant modulation by the movie.
evidence: This provides specific quantitative results from the analysis.

claim: Movie selectivity was greater than the selectivity for classic stimuli, like drifting gratings, in V1.
source: On the other hand, the movie selectivity was greater than the selectivity for classic stimuli, like drifting gratings, in V1, even within calcium imaging data, in agreement of reports of better model fit with natural stimuli for primate visual responses (David et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim compares movie selectivity to classic stimuli and is supported by citation to David et al., 2004.

claim: 33.1% of dentate gyrus neurons were significantly modulated by the movie.
source: 33.1% of dentate neurons were significantly modulated by the movie (right, green bar), far greater than chance (gray bar).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1a.

claim: 17.3% of CA3 neurons were significantly modulated by the movie.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1b.

claim: 33.6% of CA1 neurons were significantly modulated by the movie.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1c.

claim: 44.6% of subiculum neurons were significantly modulated by the movie.
source: and (d) subiculum (379/849, 44.6%) neurons.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1d.

claim: Subiculum had the largest fraction (44.6%) of movie-tuned neurons among hippocampal regions.
source: Subiculum, the output region of the hippocampus, farthest removed from the retina, had the largest fraction (44.6%, Figure 1d) of movie-tuned neurons, followed by the upstream CA1 (33.6%, Figure 1c) and DG (33.1%, Figure 1a).
evidence: This provides comparative analysis of movie tuning across hippocampal regions.

claim: CA3 movie selectivity (17.3%) was nearly half as much as other hippocampal regions.
source: However, CA3 movie selectivity was nearly half as much (17.3%, Figure 1b).
evidence: This provides comparative analysis showing CA3 has lower selectivity.

claim: Running alters neural activity in visual areas.
source: Running alters neural activity in visual areas (Niell and Stryker, 2010; Erisken et al., 2014; Christensen and Pillow, 2022; Lee et al., 2014) and hippocampus (Góis and Tort, 2018; Wiener et al., 1989; Shan et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior studies.

claim: Running alters neural activity in hippocampus.
source: Running alters neural activity in visual areas (Niell and Stryker, 2010; Erisken et al., 2014; Christensen and Pillow, 2022; Lee et al., 2014) and hippocampus (Góis and Tort, 2018; Wiener et al., 1989; Shan et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior studies.

claim: Movie tuning was unchanged when using only stationary epoch data.
source: Hence, we used the data from only the stationary epochs (see Methods) and only from sessions with at least 300 s of stationary data (17 sessions, 24,906 cells). Movie tuning was unchanged in these data (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This describes a control analysis showing movie tuning persists during immobility.

claim: Place cell spatial selectivity is greatly reduced during immobility.
source: This is unlike place cells where spatial selectivity is greatly reduced during immobility (Chen et al., 2013; Foster et al., 1989).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Chen et al., 2013 and Foster et al., 1989.

claim: Neurons recorded simultaneously from the same brain region showed different selectivity patterns.
source: Neurons recorded simultaneously from the same brain region also showed different selectivity patterns (Figure 1—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5 as evidence against nonspecific effects.

claim: Movie tuning was unaffected after removing data around sharp-wave ripples (SWRs).
source: Hence, we removed the data around SWRs and confirmed that movie tuning was unaffected (Figure 1—figure supplement 6).
evidence: This describes a control analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 6.

claim: Strong movie-tuned cells were seen in sessions with long bouts of running as well as with predominantly immobile behavior.
source: Strong movie-tuned cells were seen in sessions with long bouts of running as well as with predominantly immobile behavior (Figure 1—figure supplement 7), unlike responses to auditory tones, which were lost during running behavior (Shan et al., 2016).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 7 and compared to prior findings from Shan et al., 2016.

claim: Significant movie selectivity was found during both periods of high theta and periods of low theta.
source: We compared the movie selectivity during periods of high theta, versus periods of low theta. Significant movie selectivity in both cases (Figure 1—figure supplement 7).
evidence: This describes a control analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 7.

claim: Movie tuning was above chance levels in both high and low pupil dilation subsegments.
source: To further assess the effect of changes in brain state, we similarly analyzed movie tuning in two equal subsegments of data, corresponding to epochs with high and low pupil dilation, which is a strong correlate of arousal (Vinck et al., 2015; Schröder et al., 2020; Fekete et al., 2009). Movie tuning was above chance levels in both subsegments (Figure 1—figure supplement 7).
evidence: This describes a control analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 7, with citations supporting pupil dilation as an arousal correlate.

claim: Hippocampal neurons have one or two place-fields in typical mazes which take a few seconds to traverse.
source: Hippocampal neurons have one or two place-fields in typical mazes which take a few seconds to traverse (O'Keefe and Burgess, 1996).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to O'Keefe and Burgess, 1996.

claim: In larger arenas that take tens of seconds to traverse, the number of peaks per cell and the peak duration increases.
source: In larger arenas that take tens of seconds to traverse, the number of peaks per cell and the peak duration increases (Eliav et al., 2021; Kjelstrup et al., 2008; Harland et al., 2021; Rich et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior studies.

claim: V1 neurons had the largest number of movie-fields (mean ± SEM = 10.4 ± 0.1).
source: On average, V1 neurons had the largest number of movie-fields (Figure 2a, mean ± standard error of the mean [SEM] = 10.4 ± 0.1, here we use mean instead of median to gain a better resolution for the small and discrete values of number of fields per cell), followed by LGN (8.6 ± 0.3) and AM–PM (6.3 ± 0.07).
evidence: This provides quantitative results shown in Figure 2a.

claim: Hippocampal areas had significantly fewer movie-fields per cell: DG (2.1 ± 0.1), CA3 (2.8 ± 0.3), CA1 (2.0 ± 0.02), and subiculum (2.1 ± 0.05).
source: Hippocampal areas had significantly fewer movie-fields per cell: DG (2.1 ± 0.1), CA3 (2.8 ± 0.3), CA1 (2.0 ± 0.02), and subiculum (2.1 ± 0.05).
evidence: This provides quantitative results comparing hippocampal regions.

claim: The number of movie-fields per cell was smaller than the number of place-fields per cell in comparably long spatial tracks.
source: Thus, the number of movie-fields per cell was smaller than the number of place-fields per cell in comparably long spatial tracks (Eliav et al., 2021; Kjelstrup et al., 2008; Harland et al., 2021; Rich et al., 2014; Fenton et al., 2008; Park et al., 2011), but a handful of hippocampal cells had more than five movie-fields (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This compares current findings to prior studies on place cells, supported by multiple citations.

claim: The longest movie-fields were in subiculum (median ± SEM, 3169.9 ± 169.8 ms).
source: The longest movie-fields were in subiculum (median ± SEM, here and subsequently, unless otherwise mentioned, 3169.9 ± 169.8 ms), and the shortest in V1 (156.6 ± 9.2 ms).
evidence: This provides quantitative results shown in Figure 2b.

claim: The shortest movie-fields were in V1 (156.6 ± 9.2 ms).
source: The longest movie-fields were in subiculum (median ± SEM, here and subsequently, unless otherwise mentioned, 3169.9 ± 169.8 ms), and the shortest in V1 (156.6 ± 9.2 ms).
evidence: This provides quantitative results shown in Figure 2b.

claim: Movie-fields of LGN (308.5 ± 33.9 ms) were twice as long as in V1 (156.6 ± 9.2 ms).
source: But there were many exceptions –movie-fields of LGN (median ± SEM, here and subsequently, unless stated otherwise, 308.5 ± 33.9 ms) were twice as long as in V1 (156.6 ± 9.2 ms).
evidence: This provides quantitative comparison between LGN and V1.

claim: Movie-fields of subiculum (3169.9 ± 169.8 ms) were significantly longer than CA1 (2786.1 ± 77.5 ms).
source: Movie-fields of subiculum (3169.9 ± 169.8 ms) were significantly longer than CA1 (2786.1 ± 77.5 ms) and nearly threefold longer than the upstream CA3 (979.1 ± 241.1 ms).
evidence: This provides quantitative comparison among hippocampal regions.

claim: Movie-fields of subiculum were nearly threefold longer than CA3 (979.1 ± 241.1 ms).
source: Movie-fields of subiculum (3169.9 ± 169.8 ms) were significantly longer than CA1 (2786.1 ± 77.5 ms) and nearly threefold longer than the upstream CA3 (979.1 ± 241.1 ms).
evidence: This provides quantitative comparison among hippocampal regions.

claim: The dentate movie-fields (2113.2 ± 172.4 ms) were twofold longer than the downstream CA3.
source: However, the dentate movie-fields (2113.2 ± 172.4 ms) were twofold longer than the downstream CA3.
evidence: This provides quantitative comparison between DG and CA3.

claim: The movie-field durations spanned a 500- to 1000-fold range in every brain region investigated.
source: The movie-field durations spanned a 500- to 1000-fold range in every brain region investigated (Figure 2e).
evidence: This provides quantitative characterization of the mega-scale range shown in Figure 2e.

claim: The mega-scale range is nearly two orders of magnitude greater than previous reports in place cells.
source: This mega-scale scale is unprecedentedly large, nearly two orders of magnitude greater than previous reports in place cells (Eliav et al., 2021; Harland et al., 2021).
evidence: This compares current findings to prior studies, supported by citations.

claim: Individual neurons showed 100-fold mega-scale responses compared to less than 10-fold scale within single place cells.
source: Even individual neurons showed 100-fold mega-scale responses (Figure 2c, d) compared to less than 10-fold scale within single place cells (Eliav et al., 2021; Harland et al., 2021).
evidence: This compares current findings shown in Figure 2c,d to prior studies, supported by citations.

claim: The mega-scale tuning within a neuron was largest in V1 and smallest in subiculum.
source: The mega-scale tuning within a neuron was largest in V1 and smallest in subiculum (Figure 2e).
evidence: This provides comparative analysis shown in Figure 2e.

claim: Cumulative durations ranged from 6.2 s (V1) to 10.2 s (CA3).
source: Unlike movie-field durations, which differed by more than tenfold between hippocampal and visual regions, cumulative durations were quite comparable, ranging from 6.2 s (V1) to 10.2 s (CA3) (Figure 2f, LGN = 8.8 ± 0.21 s, V1 = 6.2 ± 0.09, AM–PM = 7.8 ± 0.09, DG = 9.4 ± 0.26, CA3 = 10.2 ± 0.46, CA1 = 9.1 ± 0.12, SUB = 9.5 ± 0.27).
evidence: This provides quantitative results shown in Figure 2f.

claim: The total duration of elevated activity was similar across all areas, spanning about a fourth of the movie.
source: Thus, hippocampal movie-fields are longer and less multi-peaked than visual areas, such that the total duration of elevated activity was similar across all areas, spanning about a fourth of the movie, comparable to the fraction of large environments in which place cells are active (Harland et al., 2021; Fenton et al., 2008; Park et al., 2011).
evidence: This provides an interpretation of the data with comparison to prior place cell studies.

claim: Net movie-field discharge was maximal in V1 and least in subiculum.
source: Unlike the tenfold variation of movie-field durations, net movie-field discharge was more comparable (<3× variation) across brain areas, but maximal in V1 and least in subiculum (Figure 2g).
evidence: This provides quantitative comparison shown in Figure 2g.

claim: Some cells showed movie-fields with elevated spiking restricted to less than 50 ms, similar to responses to briefly flashed stimuli in anesthetized cats.
source: However, some cells showed movie-fields with elevated spiking restricted to less than 50 ms, similar to responses to briefly flashed stimuli in anesthetized cats (Yen et al., 2007; Herikstad et al., 2011; Xia et al., 2021).
evidence: This describes a finding and compares it to prior studies, supported by citations.

claim: Short-duration movie-fields were common in the thalamus (LGN) and AM–PM, three synapses away from the retina.
source: Such short-duration movie-fields were not only common in the thalamus (LGN), but also AM–PM, three synapses away from the retina.
evidence: This describes the distribution of short-duration movie-fields across brain regions.

claim: A small fraction of cells in the hippocampal areas showed temporally coded fields.
source: A small fraction of cells in the hippocampal areas, more than five synapses away from the retina, showed such temporally coded fields as well (Figure 2h).
evidence: This describes a finding shown in Figure 2h.

claim: Population response stability was significantly greater for tuned than for untuned neurons.
source: Population response stability was significantly greater for tuned than for untuned neurons (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This describes a finding shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The population vector overlap around the diagonal was broader in hippocampal regions than visual cortical and LGN, indicating longer temporal-continuity.
source: The population vector overlap around the diagonal was broader in hippocampal regions than visual cortical and LGN, indicating longer temporal-continuity, reflective of their longer movie-fields.
evidence: This provides an interpretation of the population vector overlap analysis.

claim: For all brain regions, the neural F2F was correlated with image F2F.
source: For all brain regions, the neural F2F was correlated with image F2F, but this correlation was weaker in hippocampal output regions (CA1 and SUB) than visual regions like LGN and V1.
evidence: This describes the relationship between neural and image frame-to-frame correlations.

claim: The correlation between neural F2F and image F2F was weaker in hippocampal output regions (CA1 and SUB) than visual regions like LGN and V1.
source: For all brain regions, the neural F2F was correlated with image F2F, but this correlation was weaker in hippocampal output regions (CA1 and SUB) than visual regions like LGN and V1.
evidence: This describes a comparative finding across brain regions.

claim: The number of movie frames with elevated ensemble activity was higher in visual cortical areas than hippocampal regions.
source: The number of movie frames with elevated ensemble activity was higher in visual cortical areas than hippocampal regions (Figure 3d), and also this modulation (see Methods) was smaller in hippocampus and LGN, compared to the visual cortical regions (Figure 3e).
evidence: This describes comparative findings shown in Figure 3d and 3e.

claim: The degree of continuity between movie frames was inversely correlated with the ensemble rate modulation in all areas except DG, CA3, and CA1.
source: The degree of continuity between the movie frames, quantified as above (F2F image correlation), was inversely correlated with the ensemble rate modulation in all areas except DG, CA3, and CA1 (Figure 3f, g).
evidence: This describes the relationship between frame continuity and neural modulation shown in Figure 3f,g.

claim: The movie-code was stronger in the segments with greatest change across movie frames.
source: Thus, the movie-code was stronger in the segments with greatest change across movie frames, in agreement with recent reports of visual cortical encoding of flow stimuli (Dyballa et al., 2018).
evidence: This provides an interpretation of the findings with citation to a related study.

claim: The same movie frames were presented in a fixed but scrambled sequence in the scrambled movie experiment.
source: To explore this possibility, we investigated neural selectivity when the same movie frames were presented in a fixed but scrambled sequence (scrambled movie, Figure 4—video 1).
evidence: This describes the experimental design for the scrambled movie condition.

claim: There was no correlation between adjacent frames in the scrambled movie.
source: But there was no correlation between adjacent frames, i.e., visual continuity, in the latter (Figure 4a).
evidence: This describes a key property of the scrambled movie shown in Figure 4a.

claim: For all brain regions, continuous movie generated greater selectivity than scrambled sequence.
source: For all brain regions, continuous movie generated greater selectivity than scrambled sequence (KS-test p < 7.4 × 10−4).
evidence: This provides quantitative comparison with statistical significance shown in Figure 4b.

claim: The largest drop in selectivity due to scrambled movie occurred in CA1 (90.3 ± 2.0%).
source: The largest drop in selectivity due to scrambled movie occurred in CA1 (90.3 ± 2.0%), and least in V1 (−1.5 ± 0.6%).
evidence: This provides quantitative results shown in Figure 4c.

claim: Visual continuity index was significantly greater for hippocampal areas than visual (8.2-fold).
source: Visual continuity index was significantly different between all brain region pairs (KS-test p < 0.03) and significantly greater for hippocampal areas than visual (8.2-fold, p < 10−100).
evidence: This provides quantitative comparison with statistical significance.

claim: The percentage of significantly tuned hippocampal neurons (4.4%) reduced more than fourfold compared to the continuous movie (17.8%) in the scrambled condition.
source: This preference for continuous over scrambled movie was the greatest in hippocampal regions where the percentage of significantly tuned neurons (4.4%, near chance level of 2.3%) reduced more than fourfold compared to the continuous movie (17.8%, after accounting for the lesser number of trials, see Methods).
evidence: This provides quantitative comparison between continuous and scrambled conditions.

claim: The scrambled (80.4%) and the continuous movie (92.4%) generated similar prevalence levels of selectivity in visual areas.
source: This was unlike visual areas where the scrambled (80.4%) and the continuous movie (92.4%) generated similar prevalence levels of selectivity (Figure 4b).
evidence: This provides quantitative comparison shown in Figure 4b.

claim: The few hippocampal cells which had significant selectivity to the scrambled sequence had only very short, ~50-ms long responses.
source: The few hippocampal cells which had significant selectivity to the scrambled sequence, did not have long-duration responses, but only very short, ~50-ms long responses (Figure 4d), reminiscent of, but even sharper than human hippocampal responses to flashed images (Quiroga et al., 2005).
evidence: This describes a finding shown in Figure 4d with comparison to prior study.

claim: Many visual cortical neurons were significantly modulated by the scrambled sequence, but their number of movie-fields per cell was greater and their duration was shorter than during the continuous movie.
source: Many visual cortical neurons were significantly modulated by the scrambled sequence, but their number of movie-fields per cell was greater and their duration was shorter than during the continuous movie (Figure 4—figure supplements 1 and 2).
evidence: This describes findings shown in Figure 4—figure supplements 1 and 2.

claim: A substantial fraction of visual cortical and LGN responses to the scrambled sequence could be rearranged to resemble continuous movie responses.
source: A substantial fraction of visual cortical and LGN responses to the scrambled sequence could be rearranged to resemble continuous movie responses (Figure 4—figure supplement 4, see Methods).
evidence: This describes a finding shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 4.

claim: The latency needed to shift the responses was least in LGN and largest in AM–PM.
source: The latency needed to shift the responses was least in LGN and largest in AM–PM, as expected from the feed-forward anatomy of visual information processing (Siegle et al., 2021; Felleman and Van Essen, 1991; Figure 4—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This describes a finding shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 4 with citations to support the anatomical interpretation.

claim: Unlike visual areas, rearrangement did not resemble the continuous movie responses in the hippocampal regions.
source: Unlike visual areas, such rearrangement did not resemble the continuous movie responses in the hippocampal regions (example cells in Figure 4e, also see Figure 4—figure supplement 4 for statistics and details).
evidence: This describes a finding shown in Figure 4e and Figure 4—figure supplement 4.

claim: Even after rearranging the hippocampal responses, their selectivity to the scrambled movie presentation remained near chance levels.
source: Furthermore, even after rearranging the hippocampal responses, their selectivity to the scrambled movie presentation remained near chance levels (Figure 4—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This describes a finding shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 5.

claim: Continuous movie decoding was better than chance in all brain regions analyzed.
source: Continuous movie decoding was better than chance in all brain regions analyzed (Figure 4f).
evidence: This describes a finding shown in Figure 4f.

claim: Decoding was most accurate in V1, and least in DG.
source: Upon accounting for the number of tuned neurons from different brain regions, the decoding was most accurate in V1, and least in DG.
evidence: This describes a comparative finding from the decoding analysis.

claim: Scrambled movie decoding was significantly weaker yet above chance level in visual areas, but not in CA3 and DG.
source: Scrambled movie decoding was significantly weaker yet above chance level (based on shuffles, see Methods) in visual areas, but not in CA3 and DG.
evidence: This describes comparative findings from the scrambled movie decoding analysis.

claim: CA1 and subiculum neuronal ensembles could be used to decode scrambled movie frame number slightly above chance levels.
source: But CA1 and subiculum neuronal ensembles could be used to decode scrambled movie frame number slightly above chance levels (Figure 4g).
evidence: This describes a finding shown in Figure 4g.

claim: The population overlap between even and odd trials for the scrambled sequence was strong for visual areas, and weaker in hippocampal regions.
source: Similarly, the population overlap between even and odd trials for the scrambled sequence was strong for visual areas, and weaker in hippocampal regions, but significantly greater than untuned neurons in hippocampal regions (Figure 4—figure supplement 6).
evidence: This describes a finding shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 6.

claim: Loss of correlations between adjacent frames in the scrambled sequence abolishes most, but not all of the hippocampal selectivity to visual sequences.
source: Combined with the handful of neurons in hippocampus whose movie selectivity persisted to the scrambled presentation, this suggests that loss of correlations between adjacent frames in the scrambled sequence abolishes most, but not all of the hippocampal selectivity to visual sequences.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on multiple lines of evidence from the scrambled movie experiments.

claim: Movie tuning is a reliable method to probe the function of the visual brain and its role in cognition.
source: Thus, movies are a reliable method to probe the function of the visual brain and its role in cognition.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the findings showing widespread movie tuning in visual areas.

claim: A third of hippocampal neurons (32.9%, 3379/10,263) were movie tuned, comparable to the fraction of neurons with significant spatial selectivity in mice and bats.
source: Remarkably, a third of hippocampal neurons (32.9%, 3379/10,263) were also movie tuned, comparable to the fraction of neurons with significant spatial selectivity in mice (Jun et al., 2020) and bats (Yartsev et al., 2011), and far greater than significant place cells in the primate hippocampus (Rolls and O'Mara, 1995; Rolls, 2023; Mao et al., 2021).
evidence: This provides quantitative results with comparisons to prior studies, supported by citations.

claim: Hippocampal movie tuning was far greater than significant place cells in the primate hippocampus.
source: Remarkably, a third of hippocampal neurons (32.9%, 3379/10,263) were also movie tuned, comparable to the fraction of neurons with significant spatial selectivity in mice (Jun et al., 2020) and bats (Yartsev et al., 2011), and far greater than significant place cells in the primate hippocampus (Rolls and O'Mara, 1995; Rolls, 2023; Mao et al., 2021).
evidence: This provides a comparison to prior studies, supported by citations.

claim: The dissociation of the effect of mobility on spatial and movie selectivity agrees with recent reports of dissociated mechanisms of episodic encoding and spatial navigation in human amnesia.
source: This dissociation of the effect of mobility on spatial and movie selectivity agrees with the recent reports of dissociated mechanisms of episodic encoding and spatial navigation in human amnesia (McAvan et al., 2022).
evidence: This connects the current findings to prior work, supported by citation.

claim: The findings are broadly consistent with prior studies that found movie selectivity in human hippocampal single neurons.
source: Our results are broadly consistent with prior studies that found movie selectivity in human hippocampal single neurons (Gelbard-Sagiv et al., 2008).
evidence: This connects the current findings to prior work, supported by citation.

claim: Recent studies found human hippocampal activation in response to abrupt changes between different movie clips.
source: Recent studies found human hippocampal activation in response to abrupt changes between different movie clips (Zheng et al., 2022; Cohn-Sheehy et al., 2021; Reagh and Ranganath, 2023), which is broadly consistent with our findings.
evidence: This cites prior studies that are consistent with current findings.

claim: Specific visual cues can create reliable representations in all parts of hippocampus in rodents, nonhuman primates, and humans.
source: These observations support the hypothesis that specific visual cues can create reliable representations in all parts of hippocampus in rodents (Chen et al., 2013; Acharya et al., 2016; Purandare et al., 2022), nonhuman primates (Rolls and O'Mara, 1995; Mao et al., 2021), and humans (Jacobs et al., 2010; Ekstrom et al., 2003), unlike spatial selectivity which requires consistent information from multisensory cues (Moore et al., 2021; Aghajan et al., 2015; Ravassard et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a hypothesis supported by multiple citations across species.

claim: The mega-scale encoding was similar to, but far greater than recent reports of 10-fold multi-scale responses in the hippocampus.
source: Across all brain regions, neurons showed a mega-scale encoding by movie-fields varying in duration by up to 1000-fold, similar to, but far greater than recent reports of 10-fold multi-scale responses in the hippocampus (Eliav et al., 2021; Kjelstrup et al., 2008; Harland et al., 2021; Rich et al., 2014; Fenton et al., 2008; Park et al., 2011; Harland et al., 2018).
evidence: This compares current findings to prior studies, supported by citations.

claim: The average duration of the movie-field increased along the feed-forward hierarchy, consistent with the hierarchy of response lags during language processing.
source: For example, the average duration of the movie-field increased along the feed-forward hierarchy, consistent with the hierarchy of response lags during language processing (Chang et al., 2022).
evidence: This connects the current findings to prior work on language processing, supported by citation.

claim: The response latency to movie frames was highest in AM–PM (91 ms) than V1 (74 ms) and least in LGN (60 ms), following the visual hierarchy.
source: The analysis of scrambled movie-sequence allowed us to compute the neural response latency to movie frames. This was highest in AM–PM (91 ms) than V1 (74 ms) and least in LGN (60 ms), thus following the visual hierarchy.
evidence: This provides quantitative results from the scrambled movie analysis.

claim: There are other sources of inputs to V1, beyond LGN, that contribute significantly to movie tuning.
source: One possible explanation is that there are other sources of inputs to V1, beyond LGN, that contribute significantly to movie tuning (Spacek et al., 2022).
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the findings, supported by citation.

claim: Temporal integration window increases along the anatomical hierarchy in the cortex.
source: Temporal integration window (Norman-Haignere et al., 2022; Gauthier et al., 2012; Hasson et al., 2008) as well as intrinsic timescale of firing (Siegle et al., 2021) increase along the anatomical hierarchy in the cortex, with the hippocampus being farthest removed from the retina (Felleman and Van Essen, 1991).
evidence: This is a statement based on prior studies, supported by citations.

claim: The hierarchical anatomical organization could explain the longer movie-fields, the strength of tuning, number of movie peaks, their width, and decoding accuracy in hippocampal regions.
source: This hierarchical anatomical organization, with visual areas being upstream of hippocampus could explain the longer movie-fields, the strength of tuning, number of movie peaks, their width, and decoding accuracy in hippocampal regions.
evidence: This is an interpretation connecting anatomical organization to the observed findings.

claim: The several fold greater preference for the continuous movie over scrambled sequence in the hippocampus compared to the upstream visual areas could be explained by the hierarchical anatomical organization.
source: This could also explain the several fold greater preference for the continuous movie over scrambled sequence in the hippocampus compared to the upstream visual areas.
evidence: This is an interpretation connecting anatomical organization to the observed findings.

claim: The longer duration of hippocampal movie-fields could mediate visual-chunking or binding of a sequence of events.
source: These results, along with the longer duration of hippocampal movie-fields could mediate visual-chunking or binding of a sequence of events.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the findings.

claim: Evidence for episodic-like chunking of visual information was found in all visual areas as well.
source: In fact, evidence for episodic-like chunking of visual information was found in all visual areas as well, where the scrambled-sequence not only reduced neural selectivity but caused fragmentation of movie-fields (Figure 4—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This describes a finding shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 4.

claim: Poor unit isolation is unlikely to explain the brain-wide mega-scale tuning because LGN and visual cortical neural selectivity to classic stimuli in the same dataset was similar to that reported in most studies.
source: Could the brain-wide mega-scale tuning be an artifact of poor unit isolation, e.g., due to an erroneous mixing of two neurons, one with very short and another with very long movie-fields? This is unlikely since the LGN and visual cortical neural selectivity to classic stimuli (Gabor patches, drifting gratings, etc.) in the same dataset was similar to that reported in most studies (Siegle et al., 2021) whereas poor unit isolation should reduce these selective responses.
evidence: This addresses a potential confound with reference to prior work.

claim: The correlation between the unit isolation index and the mega-scale index of the cell was not significant for any brain areas.
source: However, to directly test this possibility, we calculated the correlation between the unit isolation index (or fraction of refractory violations) and the mega-scale index of the cell, while factoring out the contribution of mean firing rate (Figure 1—figure supplement 8). This correlation was not significant (p > 0.05) for any brain areas.
evidence: This describes a control analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 8.

claim: Movie-fields arising from the same mechanism as place-fields is unlikely for several reasons.
source: Do the movie-fields arise from the same mechanism as place-fields? Studies have shown that when rodents are passively moved along a linear track that they had explored (Foster et al., 1989), or when the images of the environment around a linear track was played back to them (Chen et al., 2013), some hippocampal neurons generated spatially selective activity. Since the movie clip involved change of spatial view, one could hypothesize that the movie-fields are just place-fields generated by passive viewing. This is unlikely for several reasons.
evidence: This introduces an argument against movie-fields being the same as place-fields, with citations to prior studies.

claim: Mega-scale movie-fields were found in the vast majority of all visual areas including LGN, far greater than spatially modulated neurons in the visual cortex during virtual navigation.
source: Mega-scale movie-fields were found in the vast majority of all visual areas including LGN, far greater than spatially modulated neurons in the visual cortex during virtual navigation (Haggerty and Ji, 2015; Saleem et al., 2018).
evidence: This compares current findings to prior studies, supported by citations.

claim: Compared to their spontaneous activity, about half of CA1 and CA3 neurons shutdown during spatial exploration and this shutdown is even greater in the DG.
source: Compared to their spontaneous activity, about half of CA1 and CA3 neurons shutdown during spatial exploration and this shutdown is even greater in the DG.
evidence: This is a statement about place cell behavior based on prior knowledge.

claim: Compared to the exploration of a real-world maze, exploration of a visually identical virtual world causes 60% reduction in CA1 place cell activation.
source: Furthermore, compared to the exploration of a real-world maze, exploration of a visually identical virtual world causes 60% reduction in CA1 place cell activation (Ravassard et al., 2013).
evidence: This cites a prior study showing differences between real and virtual environments.

claim: There was no evidence of neural shutdown during the movie presentation compared to gray screen spontaneous epochs.
source: In contrast, there was no evidence of neural shutdown during the movie presentation compared to gray screen spontaneous epochs (Figure 1—figure supplement 8).
evidence: This describes a finding shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 8.

claim: The number of place-fields (in CA1) per cell on a long track is positively correlated with the mean firing rate of the cell.
source: Similarly, the number of place-fields (in CA1) per cell on a long track is positively correlated with the mean firing rate of the cell (Rich et al., 2014), which was not seen here for CA1 movie-fields.
evidence: This cites a prior study and notes a difference with current findings.

claim: CA1 neurons encode the distance, angle, and movement direction of motion of a vertical bar of light.
source: A recent study showed that CA1 neurons encode the distance, angle, and movement direction of motion of a vertical bar of light (Purandare et al., 2022), consistent with the position of hippocampus in the visual circuitry (Felleman and Van Essen, 1991).
evidence: This cites a prior study with reference to anatomical organization.

claim: All the cells tuned to the moving bar of light had single receptive fields with elevated responses lasting a few seconds.
source: However, there are significant differences too; similar to place cells in the real and virtual worlds (Aghajan et al., 2015), all the cells tuned to the moving bar of light had single receptive fields with elevated responses lasting a few seconds; there were neither punctate responses nor even 10-fold variation in neural field durations, let alone the 1000-fold change reported here.
evidence: This compares current findings to a prior study, supported by citation.

claim: Hippocampal neurons did not encode Gabor patches or drifting gratings in the same dataset.
source: Notably, hippocampal neurons did not encode Gabor patches or drifting gratings in the same dataset, indicating the importance of temporally continuous sequences of images for hippocampal activation (Siegle et al., 2021).
evidence: This describes a finding with citation to the dataset source.

claim: The hippocampus is involved in coding spatial sequences.
source: This is consistent with the hypothesis that the hippocampus is involved in coding spatial sequences (Mehta, 2015; Buzsáki and Tingley, 2018; Foster and Knierim, 2012).
evidence: This connects findings to a hypothesis supported by citations.

claim: Movie-field responses without task demand would play a role, to be determined, in episodic memory.
source: We hypothesize that similar to place cells, movie-field responses without task demand would play a role, to be determined, in episodic memory.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors.

claim: The findings open up the possibility of studying thalamic, cortical, and hippocampal brain regions in a simple, passive, and purely visual experimental paradigm.
source: Our findings open up the possibility of studying thalamic, cortical, and hippocampal brain regions in a simple, passive, and purely visual experimental paradigm and extend comparable convolutional neural networks (de Vries et al., 2020) to have the hippocampus at the apex (Felleman and Van Essen, 1991).
evidence: This is a conclusion about the implications of the findings, with citations.

claim: The results bridge the long-standing gap between the hippocampal rodent and human studies.
source: Furthermore, our results here bridge the long-standing gap between the hippocampal rodent and human studies (Zheng et al., 2022; Rutishauser et al., 2006; Silson et al., 2021; King et al., 2021), where natural movies can be decoded from fMRI (functional magnetic resonance imaging) signals in immobile humans (Nishimoto et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a conclusion about the implications of the findings, with citations.

claim: Movie-coding can provide a unified platform to investigate the neural mechanisms of episodic coding, learning, and memory.
source: Thus, movie-coding can provide a unified platform to investigate the neural mechanisms of episodic coding, learning, and memory.
evidence: This is a conclusion about the broader implications of the findings.

claim: Data from 24 mice were analyzed from the Allen Brain Observatory – Neuropixels Visual Coding dataset.
source: Data from 24 mice (16 males, n = 13 C57BL/6J wild-type, n = 2 Pvalb-IRES-Cre×Ai32, n = 6 Sst-IRES-Cre×Ai32, and n = 3 Vip-IRES-Cre×Ai32) from the 'Functional connectivity' dataset were analyzed herein.
evidence: This describes the dataset used in the study.

claim: Movies were presented monocularly on an LCD monitor with a refresh rate of 60 Hz.
source: Movies were presented monocularly on an LCD monitor with a refresh rate of 60 Hz, positioned 15 cm away from the mouse's right eye and spanned 120o × 95o.
evidence: This describes the experimental setup.

claim: Thirty trials of the continuous movie presentation were followed by 10 trials of the scrambled movie.
source: Thirty trials of the continuous movie presentation were followed by 10 trials of the scrambled movie.
evidence: This describes the experimental protocol.

claim: Neural spiking data were sampled at 30 kHz with a 500-Hz high pass filter.
source: Neural spiking data were sampled at 30 kHz with a 500-Hz high pass filter.
evidence: This describes the data acquisition parameters.

claim: Spike sorting was automated using Kilosort2.
source: Spike sorting was automated using Kilosort2 (Stringer et al., 2019).
evidence: This describes the spike sorting method with citation.

claim: The movie consisted of 900 frames: 30 s total, 30 Hz refresh rate, 33.3 ms per frame.
source: The movie consisted of 900 frames: 30 s total, 30 Hz refresh rate, 33.3 ms per frame.
evidence: This describes the movie stimulus parameters.

claim: The observed sparsity was considered statistically significant if the z-scored sparsity of the observed spike train was greater 2, which corresponds to p < 0.023 in a one-tailed t-test.
source: The observed sparsity was considered statistically significant if the z-scored sparsity of the observed spike train was greater 2, which corresponds to p < 0.023 in a one-tailed t-test.
evidence: This describes the statistical criterion used for significance.
